03

Final structuresWhat did the synthesis make?

Connect morphology, diffraction and atomic structure.

Start with the measurements. TEM reveals particle shape and size; XRD probes atomic order across a population. Then explore a clearly labeled reference model.

TEM · experimental

See the particles themselves.

What shape and size did they actually make?

Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images individual particles. Here the particles are slightly prolate: longer along one axis than across it.

Long axis
3.5 nm ±5%
Short axis
3.0 nm ±6%
Elongation direction
Along (002)
HOW TO READ THIS FIGURE

Use the scale bar to read length. Dark particle outlines reveal shape; lattice contrast provides structural detail. The ±5% and ±6% describe population size spreads. The authors note that these widths are limited by uncertainty in locating particle edges.

The atomic model below uses these dimensions as its envelope. Its individual atom positions come from a separate bulk reference, not from this micrograph.

ELECTRON DIFFRACTION · P. 8711

Another check on crystal order.

Selected-area electron diffraction (SAED) also supports predominantly wurtzite order. The paper discusses it without showing a pattern and cautions that preferred orientation on the TEM grid can bias line shapes.

TEM + XRD · PP. 8710–8714

“Wurtzite” is a useful starting point.

The real particles contain stacking faults, and the diffraction analysis also considers shape and surface disorder. A perfect lattice alone does not capture every feature of these nanocrystals.

04

PropertiesWhat can these crystals do?

Follow their interaction with light.

The paper’s optical measurements link nanocrystal size to absorption and show band-edge emission. Each result stays attached to its reported sample and measurement conditions.

Absorption · experimental

Size changes the light they absorb.

How does a smaller crystal change its optical response?

Smaller CdSe nanocrystals have their lowest-energy absorption feature at shorter wavelengths. This size-dependent optical response is a signature of quantum confinement.

Reported size span
≈1.2–11.5 nm
Measurement medium
Hexane
Temperature
Room temperature
HOW TO READ THIS FIGURE

Read each size label next to its spectrum, then compare the long-wavelength absorption feature. Smaller size corresponds to a higher transition energy. The plotted amplitudes are in arbitrary units.

These are the original published curves. They are not digitized data or a predictive size-to-color slider, and the article does not supply a unique synthesis time for every curve.

FIGURE 1 · SIZE SELECTION

A narrower size distribution. Sharper absorption.

Repeated fractionation changes the illustrated population from ≈3.5 nm ±10% to ≈3.7 nm ±5% and resolves finer absorption features. This is a distinct sample series, not an optical spectrum assigned to the atomic model.

QUALITATIVE OBSERVATION · P. 8710

Emission persists in the growth solution.

The authors describe strong, sharp emission after storage in the original growth solution for over a year. This is a qualitative observation; no quantitative retention curve or lifetime is supplied.

i

Raman: not reported in the inspected main article.

No Raman spectrum is included in this example. The supporting information is still unverified. Future papers can add Raman, electrical, magnetic or other properties when their sources provide them.

SUPPORTING INFORMATION · UNRESOLVED

A matching SI file has not been verified.

The supplied collection has not yielded an identifiable SI file for this DOI. The original article has no supplementary-material notice, and a separate supplement was not verified from available publisher records. This does not establish that none exists. No later paper’s supplement is substituted here.

SOURCE LOCATORS & SCOPE

Method 1, followed through its workup.

Pages 8706–8707: general preparation and CdSe Method 1. Page 8707: isolation, purification and size-selective precipitation. Page 8708 / Figure 1: feedback and fractionation example. Page 8709 / Figure 3: absorption size series. Pages 8709–8710 / Figure 5: optical sample. Page 8710 / Figure 6: TEM dimensions. Page 8712 / Figure 11: XRD size series. Page 8714 / Figure 15: measured and simulated XRD.

CdTe Method 1 uses TOPTe and different temperatures. Method 2 uses silyl chalcogen precursors. Pyridine surface exchange is another branch. Those conditions are not merged into this CdSe recipe.

FIGURE PROVENANCE

Original measurements, with original labels.

Figures 3, 5, 6, 11 and 15 are faithful extracts of the supplied paper. Axes, internal labels and the TEM scale bar are retained; explanations are paraphrased. Figure 15 includes the original authors’ simulation alongside measured data. No spectrum or micrograph has been generated or redrawn.

SAED is described in the main text without a displayed pattern. EXAFS results are cited prior work; energy-dispersive X-ray analysis concerns discarded byproducts. Neither is presented here as a new measurement of the retained CdSe product.

Figure extraction record ↗
MOLECULAR & CRYSTAL REFERENCES

Connectivity and geometry have separate provenance.

TOP, TOPO and TOPSe are locally computed illustrative 3D conformers built from PubChem connectivity. TOP and TOPO were force-field minimized; TOPSe uses distance geometry without that minimization. Methanol and 1-butanol use PubChem computed 3D conformers. Dimethylcadmium is a connectivity schematic. The CdSe model uses an independently sourced bulk wurtzite lattice (COD 9016056); the selenium reference does not describe dissolved TOPSe. Apparatus artwork is illustrative.

MISSING OR AMBIGUOUS DETAILS

Unspecified fields remain visible.

No numerical injection duration, heating ramp, centrifugation speed or duration, or universal size–time schedule is given. The stated solution volumes total 51 mL while the syringe is described as 50 mL. Approximate 300-mg product recovery applies to the 10-mL workup aliquot and includes the organic cap.

An interactive reading of a historical method, not a ready-to-run SOP. Dimethylcadmium requires specialist laboratory handling and controls.
